generation.hypothesis: A machine-learning-driven framework that integrates existing multi-component alloy data and processing parameters will predict and optimize heat-treatment or thermo-mechanical schedules to achieve refined microstructures, stable phases, and improved mechanical properties in high-entropy alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: Homogenized or as-cast high-entropy alloys (e.g., equiatomic CrCoFeMnNi), with minimal prior deformation or secondary phases.
generation.intervention: Apply a data-driven or machine-learning model to guide process selection (e.g., temperatures, times, deformation modes), informed by existing experimental and computational HEA datasets.
generation.conditions: Thermal treatments or thermo-mechanical processing in common laboratory or industrial equipment with systematically varied durations and temperatures (e.g. 800–1200 °C) and controlled cooling rates.
generation.structural_mediator: Model-based predictions of stable phase fractions and grain boundary character distributions that promote refined microstructures and balanced mechanical properties.
generation.mechanism: By learning from prior alloy compositions, microstructures, and performance data, the machine-learning-driven framework identifies parameter-property correlations, guiding the selection of processing paths that favor stable single or multi-phase microstructures and lead to improved strength–ductility combinations.
generation.predicted_outcome: A refined microstructure, suppressed undesired secondary phases, increased mechanical strength, and enhanced ductility compared to conventional trial-and-error processing methods.
generation.baseline: Traditional incremental experimentation or CALPHAD-guided approaches that often require multiple iterative cycles to converge on suboptimal processes.
generation.boundary: Model predictions are valid primarily for compositions and temperature-pressure regimes represented in the training database; extrapolations beyond well-sampled regions remain uncertain.
generation.uncertainty: Incompleteness of alloy and process data may limit model accuracy, necessitating data augmentation or careful validation for new compositions and extreme processing conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Process a set of high-entropy alloy ingots using both the machine-learning-predicted parameters and baseline conditions, then compare the resulting microstructures and mechanical properties.

falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If a systematic discrepancy is observed between model-predicted and measured microstructures/mechanical properties, such that the predicted improvements do not outperform the baseline by a statistically significant margin, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Melting properties are critical for designing novel materials, especially for discovering high-performance, high-melting refractory materials. Experimental measurements of these properties are extremely challenging due to their high melting temperatures. Complementary theoretical predictions are, therefore, indispensable. One of the most accurate approaches for this purpose is the ab initio free-energy approach based on density functional theory (DFT). However, it generally involves expensive thermodynamic integration using ab initio molecular dynamic simulations. The high computational cost makes high-throughput calculations infeasible. Here, we propose a highly efficient DFT-based method aided by a specially designed machine learning potential. As the machine learning potential can closely reproduce the ab initio phase-space distribution, even for multi-component alloys, the costly thermodynamic integration can be fully substituted with more efficient free energy perturbation calculations. The method achieves overall savings of computational resources by 80% compared to current alternatives. We apply the method to the high-entropy alloy TaVCrW and calculate its melting properties

The concept of HEAs provides us an unprecedented degree of freedom in the design of advanced alloys with promising properties. For the rapid exploration of the vast compositional space and investigation of the composition and temperature effects on the microstructure, advanced HEA-design strategies and efficient tools are necessary. At present, a few advanced HEA-design strategies were reported by combining the physicochemical criteria, CALPHAD, data mining, and multi-objective optimization algorithm [21] , [22] , [35] – [37] , demonstrating that the CALPHAD method has played an important role in the design of advanced HEAs. There are two essential requirements to carry out calculations, using the CALPHAD method: computational software and database.

decision.trend: Early work explored mechanical alloying plus spark plasma sintering to attain refined microstructures and high strengths, albeit with challenges in controlling secondary phases and interstitial contamination. Subsequent studies leveraged heat treatments (e.g., solutionizing, aging) to manipulate ordered and disordered phases for improved strength–ductility balance. More recent investigations employ multi-step thermo-mechanical processing or high-pressure, high-temperature (HPHT) treatment to stabilize optimized microstructures, thereby achieving exceptional mechanical properties. The ongoing difficulty lies in systematically designing these processes across diverse high-entropy alloy compositions to simultaneously ensure phase stability, refine microstructures, and enhance mechanical performance.
decision.unsolved: Despite progress in refining grains and tuning phases, a universal strategy to predict and optimize processing paths for various alloy compositions remains elusive. Balancing competing requirements—such as grain refinement, phase stability, and mechanical property enhancement—across multicomponent systems still relies heavily on trial-and-error experimentation. A more comprehensive, predictive framework is needed to guide process and microstructure design.
decision.lever: Develop a machine-learning-driven framework that integrates existing high-entropy alloy data, process parameters (e.g., temperature, pressure, deformation), and target properties into a predictive model for robust process optimization.
decision.why: By learning from the vast array of prior experimental results, a data-driven model can pinpoint optimal processing conditions for phase stability and microstructure control across multiple compositions, reducing trial-and-error cycles and accelerating property optimization in high-entropy alloys.
